Thank you for submitting your article "Extracellular matrix-inducing Sox9 orchestrates basal progenitor proliferation and gliogenesis in developing neocortex" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Marianne Bronner as the Senior/Reviewing Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Joseph G Gleeson (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another. While the paper is much improved, there are remaining concerns, detailed below that need to be addressed before a final decision can be made.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript has been very nicely revised following the comments and concerns on its initial version. Unfortunately, there are still a handful of points that were not addressed properly:

Point 4:

It is very nice that the authors performed this analysis. However, it is very surprising and strange that in control electroporated cortex of mouse embryos more than 70% of RFP+pVim+ cells in SVZ-IZ are Pax6+ (less than 30% are Pax6-; new Figure 4—figure supplement 3). A large body of literature, including studies from the Huttner lab, demonstrates that the vast majority of mouse cortical BPs are bIPs, hence most mitotic cells in SVZ-IZ are Pax6-.

Point 9:

This is incorrect. Multiple comparisons tests must be performed (i.e. ANOVA) when comparing value distributions, and then only if this reveals a statistical difference one must perform t-tests bin by bin.

Point 11:

The argument of this reviewer is well understood, but the issue here is that of expression levels: direct overexpression of laminin 211 increases BP proliferation, similar to overexpression of Sox9. But is the increased expression level of Laminin α2 caused by Sox9 overexpression of sufficient magnitude to really mediate this effect? In other words, the authors' conclusions would be much stronger if they could rescue the effects of Sox9 overexpression by blockade of its effect on Laminin 211 expression levels.

Point 12:

The argument about background is acceptable, and the new high magnifications are nice, but the comment that apical mitoses are only partly visible was completely ignored. Although there is no change in apical mitosis abundance, these histological results must still be shown and demonstrated properly. The current format (same as in the previous manuscript version) is unacceptable.

Reviewer #3:

The paper has been improved by the new experiments of Sox9 CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Sox9 KO in the ferret, which are very interesting. However, I maintain a major concern about the overemphasis given to Sox9 as a "key regulator" of cortical size increase during evolution, which is not, in my opinion, supported by the data (see below). The findings remain interesting, but overemphasis in interpretation is misleading, and should be avoided.

Sox9 activation in mouse BP leads to a statistically significant, but very moderate in absolute terms, increase of BP proliferation, starting from a very low background of spontaneous (i.e. not induced by transgene) BP proliferation. The authors should take this point into serious consideration in the Discussion and throughout the paper, and substantially attenuate their proposal that Sox9 expression in BP is a key element explaining the expansion of the cortex in evolution.

The important effects shown by the KO in the ferret (though see point 2 below, to be clarified), which are certainly a worthy addition to the paper, should be reconciled with the relative ineffectiveness of Sox9 overexpression in mouse; perhaps Sox9 expression in BP in the ferret is accompanied by expression of other important factors, and it is the synergy of Sox9 with these other factors that matters in the expansion of the cortex.

In the new Figure 3 (Sox9 ko in ferret), the PCNA -mCherry/mCherry -positive cells within the VZ are reported to be numerically similar between Sox9-mutant and control ferrets (histograms in Figure 3B), however the intensity of PCNA staining in the Sox9-mutant VZ (Figure 3A) is much lower than in control. This makes one fear that the 50% reduction of PCNA-positive cells reported for the mutant OSVZ (Figure 4B) may be contributed to by a lower efficiency of the staining. This should be clarified, the image shown and the data in the histogram should be consistent.

claims.claim: Sox9 and Sox2 double-positive cells in the ISVZ and OSVZ of ferret and human neocortex comprise about half of the Sox2-positive BPs.
claims.source: Double immunofluorescence showed that virtually all Sox9-expressing cells in the ISVZ and OSVZ of E40 ferret and 15 wpc human neocortex co-expressed Sox2, implying that these cells were proliferative BPs, and that these cells comprised about half of the Sox2-positive BPs (Figure 1B,C,E,F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: 70–80% of Sox2-positive cells in the VZ of developing mouse, ferret and human neocortex also express Sox9.
claims.source: Of note, regarding the VZ of developing mouse, ferret and human neocortex, while nearly all cells were Sox2-positive, 70–80% of these also expressed Sox9 (Figure 1A–F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A-F.

claims.claim: Sox2-positive cells in the VZ that also express Sox9 are cNPCs.
claims.source: Of note, regarding the VZ of developing mouse, ferret and human neocortex, while nearly all cells were Sox2-positive, 70–80% of these also expressed Sox9 (Figure 1A–F), again in line with these cells being cNPCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the known identity of Sox2-positive cells in the VZ as cNPCs.

claims.claim: Virtually none of the Sox9-positive cells express Tbr2 in the germinal zones of E14.5 mouse, E40 ferret and 15 wpc human neocortex.
claims.source: Double immunofluorescence of the E14.5 mouse, E40 ferret and 15 wpc human neocortex for Sox9 and Tbr2 revealed that in all germinal zones, virtually none of the Sox9-positive cells expressed Tbr2, indicative of a mutually exclusive expression pattern (Figure 1G–L)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G-L.

claims.claim: Sox9 and Tbr2 exhibit a mutually exclusive expression pattern in the germinal zones of E14.5 mouse, E40 ferret and 15 wpc human neocortex.
claims.source: Double immunofluorescence of the E14.5 mouse, E40 ferret and 15 wpc human neocortex for Sox9 and Tbr2 revealed that in all germinal zones, virtually none of the Sox9-positive cells expressed Tbr2, indicative of a mutually exclusive expression pattern (Figure 1G–L)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G-L.

claims.claim: Sox9 and Sox2 double-positive cells in the VZ of mouse, ferret and human neocortex are aRG.
claims.source: Regarding the VZ, these data imply that the Sox9 and Sox2 double-positive cells observed in the three species (Figure 1D–F) are aRG
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mutually exclusive expression of Sox9 and Tbr2, and the known identity of Sox2-positive cells in the VZ.

claims.claim: Sox9-negative but Sox2-positive cells in the VZ of mouse, ferret and human neocortex are newborn BPs, notably newborn bIPs.
claims.source: whereas the Sox9-negative but Sox2-positive cells (Figure 1D–F) are newborn BPs, notably newborn bIPs
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mutually exclusive expression of Sox9 and Tbr2, and the known identity of Tbr2-positive cells as newborn bIPs.

claims.claim: Sox9 and Sox2 double-positive cells in the SVZ of ferret and human neocortex are proliferative BPs, likely bRG, rather than neurogenic bIPs.
claims.source: Regarding the SVZ, these data suggest that the Sox9 and Sox2 double-positive cells observed in ferret and human are proliferative BPs, likely bRG, rather than neurogenic bIPs.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mutually exclusive expression of Sox9 and Tbr2, and the known characteristics of different BP types.

claims.claim: Sox9 expression is down-regulated upon BPs becoming committed to neurogenesis.
claims.source: The latter conclusion in turn implies that Sox9 expression is down-regulated upon BPs becoming committed to neurogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mutually exclusive expression of Sox9 and Tbr2, where Tbr2 is a marker of neurogenic commitment.

claims.claim: The vast majority of Sox9-positive cells in the three germinal zones of P2 and P3 ferret neocortex are cycling.
claims.source: We first performed immunofluorescence for the cell cycle marker PCNA on postnatal day (P) two and P3 ferret neocortex and found that the vast majority of the Sox9-positive cells in the three germinal zones were cycling (Figure 2A,A', B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for PCNA shown in Figure 2A, 2A', and 2B.

claims.claim: The vast majority of Sox9-positive progeny in the VZ and OSVZ of P2/P3 ferret neocortex can re-enter the next cell cycle.
claims.source: We observed that the vast majority of the Sox9-positive progeny in the VZ and OSVZ can re-enter the next cell cycle at P2/P3 (Figure 2C), suggesting that the daughter cells of the EdU-labeled cNPCs maintained proliferative capacity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU pulse-chase and PCNA immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The daughter cells of EdU-labeled Sox9-positive cNPCs in ferret neocortex maintain proliferative capacity.
claims.source: We observed that the vast majority of the Sox9-positive progeny in the VZ and OSVZ can re-enter the next cell cycle at P2/P3 (Figure 2C), suggesting that the daughter cells of the EdU-labeled cNPCs maintained proliferative capacity.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the EdU pulse-chase experiment showing cell cycle re-entry.

claims.claim: Sox9-expressing BPs in the OSVZ of developing ferret neocortex exhibit a high proliferative capacity.
claims.source: We conclude that in the developing ferret neocortex, the Sox9-expressing BPs in the OSVZ, like the Sox9-expressing aRG in the VZ, exhibit a high proliferative capacity.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the cell cycle re-entry data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Essentially all mitotic aRG in the VZ of 13 wpc human neocortex are Sox9-positive.
claims.source: In 13 wpc human neocortex, essentially all mitotic aRG in the VZ and the overwhelming majority of the mitotic BPs in the SVZ were Sox9-positive (Figure 2E)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Sox9 and phospho-vimentin shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The overwhelming majority of mitotic BPs in the SVZ of 13 wpc human neocortex are Sox9-positive.
claims.source: In 13 wpc human neocortex, essentially all mitotic aRG in the VZ and the overwhelming majority of the mitotic BPs in the SVZ were Sox9-positive (Figure 2E)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Sox9 and phospho-vimentin shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Mitotic BPs in the SVZ of 13 wpc human neocortex exhibit a basal process and are bRG.
claims.source: Moreover, in line with previous observations (Fietz et al., 2010), the mitotic BPs exhibited a basal process and thus were bRG (Figure 2F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F and is consistent with previous observations (Fietz et al., 2010).

claims.claim: All mitotic bRG in the SVZ of 13 wpc human neocortex express Sox9.
claims.source: Importantly, all of the latter expressed Sox9, indicating that bRG in the fetal human neocortex are Sox9-positive (Figure 2G)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: bRG in the fetal human neocortex are Sox9-positive.
claims.source: Importantly, all of the latter expressed Sox9, indicating that bRG in the fetal human neocortex are Sox9-positive (Figure 2G)
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the immunofluorescence data showing Sox9 expression in mitotic bRG.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of Sox9 in embryonic ferret neocortex results in a strong reduction of the Sox9 protein in all germinal zones four days after in utero electroporation.
claims.source: We examined the efficiency of the knockout (KO) four days after in utero electroporation, at E37, and detected a strong reduction of the Sox9 protein in all germinal zones of the ferret neocortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B', C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, B', and C.

claims.claim: Sox9 KO in embryonic ferret neocortex results in a striking reduction in the proportion of PCNA+ cells throughout the SVZ, particularly in the OSVZ (50% reduction).
claims.source: We examined the effects of Sox9 KO on BP proliferation by immunofluorescence for PCNA, a marker of cycling cells (Figure 3A), and found a striking reduction in proportion of PCNA+ cells throughout the SVZ, and particularly in the OSVZ (50% reduction) (Figure 3B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for PCNA shown in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Sox9 KO in embryonic ferret neocortex results in a decrease in mitoses throughout the ferret germinal zones.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence of pVim (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), a marker of mitotic cells, corroborated these data, showing a decrease in mitoses throughout the ferret germinal zones (Figure 3C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for pVim shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and quantification in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Sox9 KO in embryonic ferret neocortex results in a decrease in the proportion of Sox2-positive cells with radial orientation and radial processes (bRG-like cells) in the total SVZ and particularly in the OSVZ.
claims.source: Finally, to examine if these effects pertained also to bRG, the subset of BPs that is thought to be instrumental for the evolutionary expansion of the neocortex, we focused on Sox2-positive cells in the SVZ that exhibited a radial orientation of the nucleus and the presence of radial processes (Kalebic et al., 2018) (basal and/or apical, see Figure 3—figure supplement 2, inset for examples of a bRG and a multipolar BP). We found a decrease in the proportion of these cells in the total SVZ, and in particular in the OSVZ, upon Sox9 KO (Figure 3E)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and quantification in Figure 3E, and references a citation (Kalebic et al., 2018) for the morphological criteria.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated KO of Sox9 in embryonic ferret neocortex results in a decrease of BP proliferation.
claims.source: Taken together, our data show that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated KO of Sox9 in embryonic ferret neocortex results in a decrease of BP proliferation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the PCNA, pVim, and Sox2 immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The decrease in BP proliferation upon Sox9 KO in embryonic ferret neocortex pertains to both multipolar BPs and bRG.
claims.source: Importantly, this decrease pertains to both types of BPs (multipolar BPs and bRG).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the Sox2 immunofluorescence data showing effects on both total Sox2+ BPs and bRG-like cells.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs doubles the proportion of cycling cells (Ki67+) in the SVZ and IZ at E15.5.
claims.source: Indeed, conditional Sox9 expression doubled the proportion of cells in the SVZ and intermediate zone (IZ) derived from the targeted cells (as revealed by RFP expression) that were cycling and hence were BPs, both upon analysis at E15.5 (Figure 4C,C', D,D', G) and at E14.5 (Figure 4H)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Ki67 shown in Figure 4C, C', D, D' and quantification in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs doubles the proportion of cycling cells (Ki67+) in the SVZ and IZ at E14.5.
claims.source: Indeed, conditional Sox9 expression doubled the proportion of cells in the SVZ and intermediate zone (IZ) derived from the targeted cells (as revealed by RFP expression) that were cycling and hence were BPs, both upon analysis at E15.5 (Figure 4C,C', D,D', G) and at E14.5 (Figure 4H)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Ki67 and quantification in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs markedly increases the proportion of targeted cell-derived (RFP+) BPs that undergo mitosis.
claims.source: To corroborate the effect of conditional Sox9 expression on mouse BP proliferation, we analyzed the abundance of basal mitoses by performing immunofluorescence for phospho-histone H3 one day after electroporation at E13.5 (Figure 4E,F,F'). Conditional Sox9 expression markedly increased the proportion of the targeted cell-derived (RFP+) BPs that underwent mitosis (Figure 4I)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for phospho-histone H3 shown in Figure 4E, F, F' and quantification in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: The Sox9-induced increase in the proliferation of mouse BPs pertains primarily to bIPs.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence for phospho-vimentin at E15.5 did not provide evidence that a noteworthy fraction of the targeted cell-derived (RFP+) mitotic BPs observed upon conditional Sox9 expression exhibited a prominent radial process (Figure 4J). This suggested that the Sox9-induced increase in the proliferation of mouse BPs pertained primarily to bIPs.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of prominent radial processes in RFP+ mitotic BPs, as shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs doubles the proportion of targeted cell-derived (RFP+) mitotic (pVim+) BPs that are Pax6-negative (bIPs).
claims.source: This revealed that conditional Sox9 expression doubled the proportion of the targeted cell-derived (RFP+) mitotic (pVim+) BPs that were Pax6-negative, that is bIPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for RFP, pVim, and Pax6 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, A' and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs significantly increases the proportion of targeted cell-derived (RFP+), EdU-containing cells in the SVZ plus IZ that are Ki67+ and hence cycling BPs.
claims.source: This revealed that conditional Sox9 expression significantly increased the proportion of targeted cell-derived (RFP+), EdU-containing cells in the SVZ plus IZ that were Ki67+ and hence were cycling BPs (Figure 4M)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU pulse-chase and Ki67 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4K, K', L, L' and quantification in Figure 4M.

claims.claim: The progeny of BPs exhibit an increased ability to re-enter the cell cycle upon conditional Sox9 expression.
claims.source: These data are consistent with the progeny of BPs exhibiting an increased ability to re-enter the cell cycle, that is to remain being BPs (as opposed to becoming postmitotic neurons).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the EdU pulse-chase and Ki67 immunofluorescence data showing increased cell cycle re-entry.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs decreases the abundance of Tbr2-positive cells at E15.5, especially in the SVZ.
claims.source: Tbr2 immunofluorescence of mouse neocortex electroporated at E13.5 revealed that conditional Sox9 expression decreased the abundance of Tbr2-positive cells at E15.5 (Figure 5A,B), especially in the SVZ (Figure 5A', B')
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Tbr2 shown in Figure 5A, A', B, B'.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs reduces the proportion of targeted cell-derived (RFP+) BPs in the SVZ that express Tbr2 to half.
claims.source: Specifically, conditional Sox9 expression reduced the proportion of targeted cell-derived (RFP+) BPs in the SVZ that expressed Tbr2 to half (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs may alter their identity and fate, possibly reducing their commitment to neurogenesis.
claims.source: These findings provided a first indication that conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs may alter their identity and fate, possibly reducing their commitment to neurogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reduction in Tbr2 expression upon conditional Sox9 expression.

claims.claim: Less than one fifth of Sox9-positive cells in the ISVZ and OSVZ of E40/P1 ferret neocortex are Olig2-positive.
claims.source: Double immunofluorescence for Sox9 and Olig2 of E40 ferret neocortex revealed scattered double-positive cells in the ferret ISVZ and OSVZ (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and A'), which upon quantification amounted to less than one fifth of the Sox9-positive cells in these germinal zones at E40/P1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Sox9 and Olig2 shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A' and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Essentially all Sox9-positive cells in the E40/P1 ISVZ and OSVZ of ferret neocortex are Sox2-positive and hence BPs.
claims.source: Given that essentially all Sox9-positive cells in the E40/P1 ISVZ and OSVZ of ferret neocortex are Sox2-positive (Figure 1E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,A', C) and hence BPs, we conclude that only a minority of these progenitors are committed to gliogenesis at the developmental stages studied.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', C.

claims.claim: Only a minority of Sox9-positive BPs in the ISVZ and OSVZ of E40/P1 ferret neocortex are committed to gliogenesis.
claims.source: Given that essentially all Sox9-positive cells in the E40/P1 ISVZ and OSVZ of ferret neocortex are Sox2-positive (Figure 1E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,A', C) and hence BPs, we conclude that only a minority of these progenitors are committed to gliogenesis at the developmental stages studied.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the quantification of Sox9 and Olig2 double-positive cells.

claims.claim: No Olig2 immunoreactivity is detected in the E15.5 mouse neocortical wall upon control electroporation at E13.5.
claims.source: We next examined whether mouse BPs conditionally expressing Sox9 include gliogenic precursor cells. No Olig2 immunoreactivity was detected in the E15.5 neocortical wall by immunofluorescence upon control electroporation at E13.5 (Figure 5D), in line with the onset of neocortical gliogenesis in mouse occurring later, that is around E18.5 (Miller and Gauthier, 2007)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and is consistent with the known timing of gliogenesis onset (Miller and Gauthier, 2007).

claims.claim: Upon conditional Sox9 expression for two days, many Olig2-positive cells are observed in the SVZ and IZ of E15.5 mouse neocortex.
claims.source: Remarkably, however, upon conditional Sox9 expression for two days, many Olig2-positive cells were observed in the SVZ and IZ (Figure 5E,E')
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Olig2 shown in Figure 5E, E'.

claims.claim: 22% of targeted cell-derived (RFP+) BPs in the mouse E15.5 SVZ and IZ have adopted a gliogenic identity upon conditional Sox9 expression.
claims.source: Quantification of Olig2 and RFP double-positive cells revealed that 22% of the targeted cell-derived (RFP+) BPs in the mouse E15.5 SVZ and IZ had adopted a gliogenic identity (Figure 5F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Relative Sox9 expression is highest in the High RFP population from Sox9-electroporated neocortex and much lower in the Low RFP population from the same sample.
claims.source: We first examined Sox9 mRNA levels by quantitative PCR on these sorted cell populations and observed that relative Sox9 expression was highest in the High RFP population from Sox9-electroporated neocortex and was much lower in the Low RFP population from the same sample (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Relative expression of Tbr2 mRNA is almost completely repressed in the High RFP population of Sox9-electroporated neocortex.
claims.source: We next analyzed mRNA levels for Tbr2 and Olig2 and found that relative expression of Tbr2 mRNA was almost completely repressed (Figure 5H) and relative expression of Olig2 mRNA was specifically induced (Figure 5I) in the High RFP population of Sox9-electroporated neocortex
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Relative expression of Olig2 mRNA is specifically induced in the High RFP population of Sox9-electroporated neocortex.
claims.source: We next analyzed mRNA levels for Tbr2 and Olig2 and found that relative expression of Tbr2 mRNA was almost completely repressed (Figure 5H) and relative expression of Olig2 mRNA was specifically induced (Figure 5I) in the High RFP population of Sox9-electroporated neocortex
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: High Sox9 levels in mouse BPs induce a switch in their cell fate to gliogenesis by inducing Olig2 mRNA and repressing Tbr2 mRNA expression.
claims.source: We conclude that high Sox9 levels in mouse BPs induce a switch in their cell fate to gliogenesis by inducing Olig2 mRNA and repressing Tbr2 mRNA expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the qPCR data showing dose-dependent effects of Sox9 on Tbr2 and Olig2 expression.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs increases the percentage of RFP+ cells in the SVZ that are Sox2-positive at E14.5.
claims.source: Quantification of the percentage of the RFP+ cells in the SVZ that were Sox2-positive revealed an increase upon Sox9 expression (Figure 5L)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Sox2 shown in Figure 5J, K and quantification in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: Upon conditional Sox9 expression at E13.5, 10–15% of the RFP+ cells in the SVZ are still positive for Tbr2 at E15.5.
claims.source: Given that upon conditional Sox9 expression at E13.5, 10–15% of the RFP+ cells in the SVZ are still positive for Tbr2 at E15.5 (Figure 5C), this observation suggests that the increased number of BPs consist of a mix of neurogenic and gliogenic progenitors.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The increased number of BPs upon conditional Sox9 expression consists of a mix of neurogenic and gliogenic progenitors.
claims.source: Given that upon conditional Sox9 expression at E13.5, 10–15% of the RFP+ cells in the SVZ are still positive for Tbr2 at E15.5 (Figure 5C), this observation suggests that the increased number of BPs consist of a mix of neurogenic and gliogenic progenitors.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the presence of both Tbr2+ and Sox2+ cells among RFP+ BPs.

claims.claim: Differential gene expression analysis comparing conditionally Sox9 expressing vs control High RFP cells yielded 749 downregulated and 870 upregulated protein-encoding genes (q < 0.01).
claims.source: In order to identify the genes that were affected by conditional Sox9 expression, we performed differential gene expression (DGE) analysis by comparing the expression levels of only protein-encoding genes in conditionally Sox9 expressing vs control High RFP cells. This yielded 749 downregulated and 870 upregulated protein-encoding genes upon Sox9 expression (q < 0.01) (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: GO term enrichment analysis of the 870 genes upregulated in Sox9-expressing cells revealed that the highest enrichment scores most frequently included genes related to the ECM.
claims.source: To gain insight into the cell biological processes affected by conditional Sox9 expression, we examined the 870 genes upregulated in Sox9-expressing cells by gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis for biological process (Figure 6C) and cellular component (Figure 6D). This analysis revealed that the highest enrichment scores most frequently included genes related to the ECM (Figure 6C and D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: KEGG pathway analysis of the 870 genes upregulated in Sox9-expressing cells yielded the highest enrichment scores for ECM production, organization and degradation.
claims.source: Similarly, KEGG pathway analysis using the same gene set as input yielded the highest enrichment scores for ECM production, organization and degradation (Figure 6E)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: 203 of the 870 genes upregulated in Sox9-expressing cells are related to the ECM.
claims.source: GO term enrichment and KEGG pathway analyses indicated that 203 of the 870 genes upregulated in Sox9-expressing cells were related to the ECM (Figure 6C–E, Supplementary file 3)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment and KEGG pathway analyses shown in Figure 6C-E and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression induces the expression of gliogenic genes such as Olig2 and S100b.
claims.source: In addition to the upregulation of expression of ECM components, conditional Sox9 expression induced the expression of gliogenic genes such as Olig2 and S100b (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), corroborating the effect of conditional Sox9 expression on gliogenesis observed by immunohistochemistry (Figure 5E and F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B, and is consistent with immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in significant increases in the numbers of Ki67-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ.
claims.source: Quantification per unit area of the numbers of Ki67-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ (Figure 7D), of PH3-positive and RFP-negative abventricular mitoses (Figure 7E), and of Sox2-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ (Figure 7F) revealed significant increases for all three cell populations in conditionally Sox9-expressing neocortex
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in significant increases in the numbers of PH3-positive and RFP-negative abventricular mitoses.
claims.source: Quantification per unit area of the numbers of Ki67-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ (Figure 7D), of PH3-positive and RFP-negative abventricular mitoses (Figure 7E), and of Sox2-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ (Figure 7F) revealed significant increases for all three cell populations in conditionally Sox9-expressing neocortex
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in significant increases in the numbers of Sox2-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ.
claims.source: Quantification per unit area of the numbers of Ki67-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ (Figure 7D), of PH3-positive and RFP-negative abventricular mitoses (Figure 7E), and of Sox2-positive and RFP-negative nuclei in SVZ+IZ (Figure 7F) revealed significant increases for all three cell populations in conditionally Sox9-expressing neocortex
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in a cell non-autonomous stimulation of BP proliferation.
claims.source: These findings indicate that conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs not only increases their proliferation cell-autonomously (see Figure 4), but also results in a cell non-autonomous stimulation of BP proliferation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the increased proliferation of RFP-negative BPs upon conditional Sox9 expression.

claims.claim: The percentage of NeuN-positive nuclei in the CP is significantly increased upon conditional Sox9 expression at E17.5.
claims.source: Specifically, we performed immunofluorescence for NeuN at E17.5 of mouse neocortex electroporated at E13.5 (Figure 7G and H), and found that the percentage of NeuN-positive nuclei in the CP was significantly increased upon conditional Sox9 expression (Figure 7I)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for NeuN shown in Figure 7G, H and quantification in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in BPs results in a significant increase in the percentage of nuclei in the CP that are RFP-negative and NeuN-positive.
claims.source: Further examination of the NeuN-positive nuclei in the CP showed that conditional Sox9 expression in BPs resulted in a significant increase in the percentage of nuclei that were RFP-negative and NeuN-positive (Figure 7K)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7K.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in increased neuron production from BPs whose proliferation was stimulated in a cell non-autonomous manner.
claims.source: Taken together, we conclude that conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in increased neuron production from BPs whose proliferation was stimulated in a cell non-autonomous manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the increased NeuN-positive, RFP-negative neurons in the CP.

claims.claim: Conditional Sox9 expression in BPs results in a significant, more than two-fold increase in the number of EdU+ Satb2+ RFP- cells in the CP at E17.5.
claims.source: On the one hand, conditional Sox9 expression in BPs resulted in a significant, more than two-fold increase in the number EdU-containing (EdU+) cells in the CP that were Satb2-positive and RFP-negative, that is progeny derived from of non-electroporated cells (Figure 7O)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Satb2 and EdU shown in Figure 7L, M and quantification in Figure 7O.

claims.claim: The proportion of EdU+ RFP+ cells that are Tbr1+ is massively decreased upon conditional Sox9 expression in BPs at E17.5.
claims.source: In contrast, the proportion of EdU-containing (EdU+) RFP-positive (RFP+) cells that were Tbr1-positive (Tbr1+) was found to be massively decreased upon conditional Sox9 expression in BPs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data for Tbr1 and EdU shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B and quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Upon conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs, the production of upper-layer neurons is increased and this increase involves the non-targeted BPs whose proliferation is stimulated in a cell non-autonomous manner.
claims.source: We conclude that upon conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs the production of upper-layer neurons is increased and that this increase involves the non-targeted BPs whose proliferation is stimulated in a cell non-autonomous manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the increased Satb2+ RFP- neurons and decreased Tbr1+ RFP+ neurons.

claims.claim: Upon conditional Sox9 expression in BPs, the relative distribution of RFP+ cells in the CP is shifted towards the upper layers, with a significant decrease in the percentage of RFP+ cells in the lower layers (bin 2) and an increase in the upper layers (bin 7) at E18.5.

results.result: Sox9 mRNA and protein expression patterns differ between mouse, ferret, and human developing neocortex. In mouse, Sox9 is restricted to the VZ and expressed in aRG but not BPs. In ferret and human, Sox9 is expressed in VZ, ISVZ, and OSVZ, including in BPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 are well-supported by transcriptome data (FPKM values) from published datasets and immunofluorescence imaging across three species. The data consistently show species-specific differences in Sox9 expression patterns, with mouse showing VZ-restricted expression while ferret and human show broader SVZ expression. The nuclear localization and BP expression in gyrencephalic species are clearly documented.

results.result: Sox9-expressing cells in the SVZ of ferret and human neocortex co-express Sox2, identifying them as proliferative BPs. These Sox9+Sox2+ cells comprise approximately half of Sox2+ BPs in the SVZ, and 70-80% of VZ Sox2+ cells also express Sox9.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 are supported by double immunofluorescence data with quantification shown in Figure 1. The co-expression patterns are clearly demonstrated, and the quantitative assessments provide specific percentages. The inference that these are proliferative BPs/cNPCs is reasonable based on established Sox2 expression patterns.

results.result: Sox9 and Tbr2 show mutually exclusive expression in germinal zones across mouse, ferret, and human neocortex. This pattern indicates that Sox9+Sox2+ cells in the VZ are aRG, while Sox9-Sox2+ cells are newborn bIPs, and Sox9+Sox2+ cells in the SVZ are proliferative BPs (likely bRG) rather than neurogenic bIPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 are well-supported by double immunofluorescence data (Figure 1G-L) showing mutually exclusive expression patterns. The inferences about cell identity (C20-C22) are reasonable based on established marker expression profiles, though they rely on known literature rather than direct functional validation in this study. The conclusion about Sox9 downregulation during neurogenic commitment (C23) is a logical inference from the Tbr2 exclusion pattern.

results.result: Sox9-expressing cells in ferret neocortex are highly proliferative. The vast majority are cycling (PCNA+) and can re-enter the cell cycle after division, indicating that Sox9-expressing BPs in the OSVZ exhibit high proliferative capacity similar to aRG in the VZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by PCNA immunofluorescence and EdU pulse-chase experiments (Figure 2A-C). The cell cycle re-entry data provide direct evidence for proliferative capacity. However, the time intervals between EdU administration and analysis could be better justified based on known cell cycle lengths.

results.result: In human fetal neocortex, essentially all mitotic aRG and the overwhelming majority of mitotic BPs are Sox9-positive. Mitotic BPs in the SVZ are bRG (exhibiting basal processes), and all mitotic bRG express Sox9.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by immunofluorescence for Sox9 and phospho-vimentin in human tissue (Figure 2D-G). The identification of bRG by basal process morphology is consistent with established criteria (Fietz et al., 2010). The quantification shows clear Sox9 expression in mitotic cells.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of Sox9 in embryonic ferret neocortex reduces BP proliferation. Sox9 KO results in decreased PCNA+ cells (50% reduction in OSVZ), decreased mitoses, and reduced Sox2+ bRG-like cells, affecting both multipolar BPs and bRG.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing Sox9 protein reduction and decreased proliferation markers (Figure 3, Figure 3-supplements). The CRISPR/Cas9 approach is validated by showing Sox9 protein reduction. Multiple proliferation markers (PCNA, pVim, Sox2) consistently show decreased BP proliferation. Statistical significance is reported for key measurements.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs doubles the proportion of cycling cells and increases basal mitoses. The Sox9-induced proliferation increase pertains primarily to bIPs, and BP progeny show increased cell cycle re-entry ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 are supported by multiple proliferation assays (Ki67, PH3, EdU pulse-chase) with statistical significance reported (Figure 4). The identification of bIPs as the primary affected population is supported by morphological analysis (lack of radial processes) and Pax6 staining. The cell cycle re-entry data provide evidence for sustained proliferative capacity.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs decreases Tbr2 expression, particularly in the SVZ, reducing the proportion of Tbr2+ BPs by half. This suggests Sox9 may alter BP identity and fate, possibly reducing neurogenic commitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by Tbr2 immunofluorescence with quantification (Figure 5A-C). The reduction in Tbr2 expression is statistically significant. The inference about altered identity and reduced neurogenic commitment (C49) is reasonable given Tbr2's role as a neurogenic marker, though it remains somewhat speculative without direct fate-mapping.

results.result: In ferret neocortex at E40/P1, less than one-fifth of Sox9+ cells in ISVZ/OSVZ are Olig2+, and essentially all Sox9+ cells are Sox2+ BPs. This indicates only a minority of Sox9+ BPs are committed to gliogenesis at these developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by double immunofluorescence for Sox9/Olig2 and Sox9/Sox2 with quantification (Figure 5-supplement 1). The data clearly show limited Olig2 co-expression with Sox9, supporting the conclusion about minority gliogenic commitment. However, this is a snapshot at specific timepoints and may not capture dynamic changes.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs induces premature gliogenesis. While no Olig2 is detected in control E15.5 neocortex, Sox9 expression for two days results in many Olig2+ cells in SVZ/IZ, with 22% of targeted BPs adopting gliogenic identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by Olig2 immunofluorescence (Figure 5D-F). The absence of Olig2 in controls is consistent with known timing of mouse gliogenesis (Miller and Gauthier, 2007). The appearance of Olig2+ cells upon Sox9 expression is striking and well-quantified, demonstrating premature gliogenic fate switch.

results.result: High Sox9 levels in mouse BPs induce a dose-dependent switch to gliogenesis by inducing Olig2 mRNA and repressing Tbr2 mRNA. The High RFP population shows highest Sox9 expression, almost complete Tbr2 repression, and specific Olig2 induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by qPCR analysis of FACS-sorted cell populations (Figure 5-supplement 2C, Figure 5H-I). The dose-dependent relationship between Sox9 levels and fate markers is clearly demonstrated. The conclusion about Sox9-induced gliogenic switch (C59) is well-supported by the molecular data, though functional validation would strengthen it.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression increases Sox2+ cells in the SVZ at E14.5. Given that 10-15% of RFP+ cells remain Tbr2+ at E15.5, the increased BP population consists of a mix of neurogenic and gliogenic progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by Sox2 immunofluorescence (Figure 5J-L) and reference to earlier Tbr2 data (Figure 5C). The inference about mixed neurogenic/gliogenic populations (C62) is reasonable based on the marker expression patterns, though direct demonstration of both fates in the same lineage would be more definitive.

results.result: Transcriptome analysis reveals that conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs predominantly upregulates ECM-related genes. Of 870 upregulated genes, 203 are ECM-related, with highest enrichment for ECM organization, production, and degradation pathways. Sox9 also induces gliogenic genes (Olig2, S100b).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by RNA-seq analysis with appropriate bioinformatics (Figure 6, Figure 6-supplement 2). The differential expression analysis uses appropriate statistical cutoffs (q<0.01). GO term and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses consistently identify ECM-related processes. The gliogenic gene induction corroborates immunofluorescence findings. Sample clustering shows clear separation between conditions.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs results in cell non-autonomous stimulation of BP proliferation. Significant increases are observed in Ki67+ RFP- cells, PH3+ RFP- mitoses, and Sox2+ RFP- cells in SVZ+IZ, indicating proliferation of non-targeted BPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by quantification of RFP-negative proliferating cells (Figure 7A-F). The use of RFP as a lineage marker allows clear distinction between targeted and non-targeted cells. Multiple proliferation markers consistently show cell non-autonomous effects. Statistical significance is reported. The conclusion about non-autonomous stimulation (C71) is well-supported.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression in mouse BPs increases neuron production, particularly from non-targeted BPs. The percentage of NeuN+ nuclei in CP increases significantly, with a specific increase in RFP-negative NeuN+ neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by NeuN immunofluorescence at E17.5 (Figure 7G-K). The increase in total NeuN+ neurons and specifically RFP-negative NeuN+ neurons is statistically significant. The conclusion about increased neuron production from non-autonomously stimulated BPs (C74) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression increases upper-layer neuron production from non-targeted BPs. There is a >2-fold increase in Satb2+ RFP- EdU+ cells, while Tbr1+ RFP+ EdU+ cells are massively decreased, indicating increased upper-layer and decreased deep-layer neuron production.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by EdU pulse-chase combined with layer marker immunofluorescence (Figure 7L-O, Figure 7-supplement 1). The opposing effects on upper-layer (Satb2+) and deep-layer (Tbr1+) markers are clearly demonstrated with statistical significance. The conclusion about non-autonomous effects on upper-layer neuron production (C77) is well-supported.

results.result: At E18.5, conditional Sox9 expression shifts RFP+ cell distribution toward upper CP layers and decreases Tbr1+ RFP+ cells. There are significant increases in Satb2+ RFP- cells and total Satb2+ cells, with the increase pertaining mostly to non-electroporated cell progeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are supported by layer distribution analysis and marker quantification at E18.5 (Figure 8). The shift in RFP+ cell distribution is statistically significant for specific bins. The changes in Tbr1+ and Satb2+ populations are well-quantified. The conclusion about non-autonomous effects (C82) is consistent with the RFP-negative cell increases.

results.result: Conditional Sox9 expression increases expression of laminin and collagen mRNAs. Laminin α2 shows ~2-fold increase, Lamb1 and Lamc1 are expressed at levels consistent with laminin 211 formation, and collagen 4α1 shows >3-fold increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by RNA-seq FPKM values (Figure 9A-D). The increases in ECM component mRNAs are consistent with the broader transcriptome analysis showing ECM upregulation. However, the claim about laminin 211 formation (C84) is inferential based on subunit expression levels without direct protein complex validation.

results.result: Laminin 211, but not collagen IV, promotes BP proliferation in organotypic slice cultures. Laminin 211 causes significant increase in Ki67+ cells specifically in SVZ and strikingly increases basal mitoses, while apical mitoses are unaffected by either ECM component.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by organotypic slice culture experiments with recombinant ECM proteins (Figure 9E-G). The specific effect of laminin 211 on SVZ proliferation and basal mitoses is clearly demonstrated with statistical significance. This provides direct functional evidence linking ECM components to BP proliferation. Sample size appears adequate (n=3 embryos).

results.result: Sox9 is a major inducer of ECM components, and the cell non-autonomous stimulation of BP proliferation by Sox9 is likely mediated by secreted ECM components acting on neighboring BPs in autocrine and paracrine manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 integrate multiple lines of evidence: transcriptome showing ECM upregulation (C90), organotypic culture showing laminin effects on proliferation, and cell non-autonomous proliferation effects. The conclusion about Sox9 as ECM inducer (C90) is well-supported. The mechanism proposed for non-autonomous effects (C91) is reasonable but somewhat speculative, as direct evidence for secretion and paracrine signaling is not provided.

results.result: Sox9 has three major effects: promoting BP proliferation both cell-autonomously and non-autonomously, increasing upper-layer neuron production, and switching BPs to gliogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are summary statements integrating multiple experimental findings. Each is well-supported by the data: C92 by proliferation assays in targeted and non-targeted cells, C93 by Satb2+ neuron quantification, and C94 by Olig2 induction. These represent the major conclusions of the study.

results.result: Sox9 shows hallmarks of a transcription factor contributing to neocortical expansion. Upper-layer neuron increase is a hallmark of expansion, Sox9 has established roles in adult neurogenesis and embryonic layer generation, and neocortical expansion involves both neurogenesis and gliogenesis increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 integrate current findings with established literature. C95, C98 cite appropriate references for general principles. C96-C97, C99 cite specific prior studies. The synthesis conclusion (C100) is reasonable given the demonstrated effects on proliferation, ECM, neurogenesis, and gliogenesis, though it remains somewhat speculative regarding evolutionary relevance.

results.result: Neocortical expansion is linked to increased BP proliferative capacity and pool size. In non-expanded cortices (mouse), BPs have low proliferative capacity and thin SVZ. In expanded cortices (human), BPs have high proliferative capacity and thick SVZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 are background knowledge claims supported by extensive citations. These represent well-established principles in the field and provide appropriate context for the study. The citations are appropriate and comprehensive.

results.result: ECM component expression differs between mouse and human neocortex. In mouse, BPs downregulate ECM compared to aRG, and ECM expression is downregulated in SVZ vs VZ. In human, ECM expression is maintained in VZ, ISVZ, and OSVZ, with both aRG and bRG showing characteristic ECM expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are based on appropriate citations of prior work (Arai et al., 2011; Fietz et al., 2012; Florio et al., 2015; Pollen et al., 2015). These provide important background for the study's hypothesis about Sox9 and ECM regulation.

results.result: ECM-integrin signaling promotes BP proliferation. Integrin αvβ3 activation promotes mouse BP proliferation, its inhibition reduces ferret BP pool size, BPs in expanded cortices have increased processes for integrin signaling, and integrin β1 blocking reduces human BP proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C112 are based on appropriate citations including prior work by the authors (Stenzel et al., 2014; Fietz et al., 2010; Kalebic et al., 2019). These establish the ECM-integrin-proliferation axis that motivates the current study. The general concept (C112) is well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Sox9 was identified as a candidate ECM driver in human SVZ through in silico analysis. Sox9 is known to drive glia-specific gene expression and mediate the neurogenesis-to-gliogenesis switch in developing spinal cord.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 provide the rationale for studying Sox9. C113 cites the in silico analysis (Fietz et al., 2012) that motivated the study. C114-C115 cite appropriate literature on Sox9's known roles in gliogenesis, providing context for the gliogenic effects observed.

results.result: Neurogenesis and gliogenesis timing differs between species. In mouse, they occur sequentially with gliogenesis after neurogenesis. In gyrencephalic species (human, macaque, ferret), neurogenic and gliogenic progenitors co-exist at later neurogenesis stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These establish important species differences in developmental timing that contextualize the premature gliogenesis findings in the Sox9 experiments.
